div.p: The sampling periods of real-time embedded control functions have a significant impact on control performance and system schedulability. Exploring period assignment for optimizing control performance while meeting schedulability constraints is very challenging, in particular for distributed systems where control loops share computation and communication resources. We propose an efficient approach that approximates the performance of each control loop in the system with a piecewise linear function of its sampling period and end-toend delay, and then optimizes the periods of tasks and messages by exploring the linear partitions of the approximated functions and solving a series of geometric programming (GP) formulations.

div.head: OVERVIEW
div.p: In real-time embedded control systems, optimizing the period assignments while guaranteeing schedulability is crucial for system performance and reliability. Previous period assignment approaches either focus on uniprocessor systems, or use randomized search methods (e.g. genetic algorithms, simulated annealing), which are prone to end up in local minima and may require long running time for large-size problems. In this work, we propose an efficient geometric programming based approach to optimize the task and message periods for control performance on a distributed CAN-based (Controller Area Networks) platform. The algorithm enables solving systems with large design spaces, possible runtime reconfiguration, and architecture exploration.

Fig. 1 shows the flow of our control-driven period optimization algorithm. The approach approximates the performance of each control path J i with a piecewise linear function J ′ i of sampling period T i and end-to-end delay l i , and then explores the period assignments by solving a series of mixed integer geometric programming (MIGP) problems, each of which is formed by selecting linear partitions from the piecewise linear functions. We solve the MIGP problem using the similar iterative approach proposed in [1], which approximates the MIGP with continuous-variable GP and iteratively improves the approximation. Experiments from an industrial case study and synthetic examples demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach -it provides better control performance than other GP-based approaches, and better efficiency than a simulated annealing algorithm we developed (with similar performance).
